Chapter 1: Growing Up in a World of Certainty and Control
Picture this: you’re living in a place where every part of your day—where you live, what you believe, even how you feel about your country’s leaders—is decided for you. In North Korea, the state shapes the rhythm of life in ways most of us can hardly imagine. From the moment you’re born, your path is already set. The outside world? It’s just a rumor—something you might hear about, but never see. And questioning any of this? That feels as far away as the moon.
Now, let’s zoom in on the city of Chongjin, a bustling industrial spot on the coast. Here, families wake up to patriotic songs pouring out of loudspeakers. The day kicks off with rituals of loyalty. Kids recite oaths to the leaders at school, workers gather for group exercises and political lectures. Every home has portraits of the country’s founder and his son—the current leader—hanging on the wall, carefully cleaned each day. If you’re a student here, the world feels solid and unchanging: the leaders are wise, the country is mighty, and the world outside? Well, that’s a dangerous place you’re better off not thinking about.
Imagine a teacher in this city—someone who’s proud, dedicated, and truly believes in the system. She spends her days shaping young minds, trusting she’s part of something bigger. Her students soak up stories about their country’s history and the dangers of its enemies. At home, she’s just as careful, always avoiding any hint of disloyalty. Even chatting with neighbors? That’s measured—you never know who might be listening in.
But if you look a little closer, you’ll notice small cracks in the surface. There’s a factory worker, once proud to help build the nation, now standing in silence as the machines slow down and parts run out. He waits in line for food rations that seem to shrink every month, but he keeps his doubts to himself. At night, families gather around their radios, but the dials are stuck on government stations. Curiosity about what’s beyond the border? That’s risky, and most folks learn early on to push those questions aside.
Still, every now and then, something doesn’t add up. A mother wonders why her cousin in the countryside looks thinner every time she visits. A student hears a whispered joke about the leaders and feels that mix of fear and excitement. These moments are quick, private—and they’re usually buried under the weight of daily routine. For most people, comfort comes from the familiar—the rituals that shape every day and give life some meaning.
There’s a real sense of community here, but it’s built on everyone watching everyone else. Neighbors are supposed to report anything suspicious, and even kids are taught to keep an eye out for signs of disloyalty. Trust? That’s something you can’t afford easily. Friendships are careful, conversations are guarded, because just one careless word could cost you your job, bring a visit from the authorities, or lead to something even worse.
But even with all this pressure, people still manage to carve out tiny pockets of normal life. Picture a grandmother tending a little garden behind her apartment, coaxing a few vegetables from tired soil. Or a group of teenagers sneaking off to the riverbank, sharing stories and dreams they’d never say out loud. In these quiet moments, the human spirit finds a way—adapting, holding on, even when real freedom feels like a distant memory.
Over time, the system’s boundaries become part of you. Most people don’t even notice how tightly their lives are shaped—they just do what’s expected, finding meaning in family, work, and the daily routines. The outside world stays in the shadows, showing up only in rumors or the rare, forbidden broadcast. For those who grow up here, the idea of ever questioning the system isn’t just dangerous—it almost feels impossible.
